client: I've been really struggling since I started college last semester — the workload is just so much more than I expected, and I feel like I'm constantly behind no matter how hard I try. It's gotten to the point where I've kind of pulled away from the few friends I made at the beginning of the year, because I feel like I don't have time for anything except trying to catch up. Honestly, I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change anything, but I figured I had to try something.
therapist: It sounds like you're carrying a really heavy load right now — feeling perpetually behind while also losing the social connections that could help you recharge is an exhausting combination, and it makes sense that you're feeling worn down. I'm also glad you reached out, even with that doubt in the back of your mind, because that small step actually tells me something important about your resilience. When you say you feel "constantly behind no matter how hard you try," I'm curious — what does that inner voice usually tell you about *why* that's happening?

client: Honestly, that inner voice is pretty brutal — it basically tells me I'm just not smart enough to be here, like everyone else figured out how to handle college and I somehow missed the memo. There's this constant feeling that I should be able to manage this on my own, and the fact that I can't just proves I don't belong here. It's hard to even say that out loud because it sounds so dramatic, but it's genuinely what I think most of the time.
therapist: What you just shared takes real courage, and I want you to know it doesn't sound dramatic at all — it sounds like a thought pattern that's been quietly convincing you of something very painful that deserves to be examined. In CBT, we call these kinds of thoughts "cognitive distortions," and the one you're describing — using struggle as *proof* that you don't belong — is actually one of the most common ones college students experience, which itself is worth sitting with for a moment. If a close friend came to you and said "I'm struggling with the workload, so I must not be smart enough to be here," what would you say back to them?

client: I'd obviously tell a friend that struggling doesn't mean they don't belong, that college is hard for everyone and it doesn't say anything about their intelligence. But I already know what you're going to say — that I should apply that same logic to myself — and honestly, it feels different when it's me. Like, I can see the logic of it, but it doesn't actually make the feeling go away, you know?
therapist: You've actually just identified something really important — that knowing something logically and *feeling* it emotionally are two very different things, and that gap is real, not a sign that you're doing this wrong. That disconnect is something we work with directly in CBT, because you're right that insight alone doesn't rewire the feeling; it takes practice building new experiences that gradually make the compassionate thought *feel* true, not just sound true. I'm wondering — can you think of even one moment this semester, however small, where you handled something difficult in a way that doesn't quite fit the story that you don't belong here?

client: There was this one time a few weeks ago where I had three assignments due in the same week and I actually got them all in on time, even though I was running on barely any sleep. But the thing is, my brain immediately went to "yeah but your grades probably weren't great" before I even got the results back, so it didn't really feel like a win. I guess I have a hard time letting anything count as evidence that I'm doing okay.
therapist: What you just described — managing three assignments in one brutal week on almost no sleep — is genuinely impressive, and I want to gently point out what your brain did: it moved the goalposts *before you even had the evidence*, which meant there was no possible outcome that could count as a win. That's a really telling pattern, and it's worth naming — it's not that you lack evidence you're doing okay, it's that there's a part of you that's been filtering it out before it can land. What do you think that part of you is trying to protect you from, by refusing to let the wins count?

client: That's a question I haven't really thought about before, and my gut reaction is... maybe it's protecting me from getting my hopes up and then being blindsided when things fall apart? Like if I never let myself believe I'm doing okay, then failing won't feel as devastating because I already expected it. But even as I say that, I realize it also means I'm basically guaranteeing I feel terrible all the time, which doesn't really make sense as a strategy.
therapist: That insight you just had is genuinely significant — you've essentially caught your own mind in a trade-off where it's accepting *constant* pain as the price of avoiding *occasional* pain, which when you say it out loud, doesn't quite hold up. This is actually a really common protective strategy that made sense at some point, probably when disappointment felt really unsafe, but it's now costing you more than it's saving you. I'm curious — as you sit with that realization, does it shift anything, even slightly, in how you feel about letting that one small win from a few weeks ago actually count?

client: Maybe a little, yeah — like, when I actually let myself think about it, getting those three assignments done under that kind of pressure was genuinely hard, and I did it. But there's still this nagging feeling that one moment doesn't really change the bigger picture, like it's an exception rather than proof of anything. I guess I'm just not sure how to get from acknowledging one small win to actually feeling like I belong here in any lasting way.
therapist: That "maybe a little" is actually more meaningful than it might feel right now — you let something in, even briefly, and that's exactly how this process works, not in one dramatic shift but in small moments of letting evidence land. The feeling that one win is "just an exception" is actually the distortion defending itself, because that's what it does — it protects its own story by framing every contradiction as a fluke. What if, instead of needing one moment to change everything, we started small — like just noticing and collecting these "exceptions" over the coming weeks, almost like building a case file against the belief that you don't belong?

client: I like the idea of it in theory, but I'm a little skeptical about whether I'd actually follow through — like, my brain is so quick to dismiss things in the moment that I'm not sure I'd even recognize a win when it's happening, let alone remember to write it down. And honestly, with how overwhelmed I already feel, adding another thing to my plate, even a small one, feels a bit daunting. How does this actually work in practice without it just becoming another thing I feel guilty about not doing?
therapist: Your skepticism is really valid, and honestly, the fact that you're thinking practically about what will actually work for you rather than just agreeing to something is a good sign — that's self-awareness, not resistance. The last thing we want is another stick to beat yourself with, so let's make this as low-friction as possible: it doesn't need to be a journal or a daily habit, it could be as simple as sending yourself a one-line text in a moment when something goes okay, just enough to create a small record your brain can't as easily erase. What would feel like the *least* burdensome version of this that you might actually do?

client: The text idea actually feels more manageable than I expected, like it's low enough stakes that I might actually do it. I think I could probably manage sending myself something short when a moment happens, even if it's just "handed in that paper" or whatever. My only worry is that I'll look back at those texts later and still find a way to talk myself out of them mattering, but I guess that's kind of the whole problem we're trying to work on, isn't it.
therapist: You just answered your own worry in the same breath you raised it, which is actually a really good sign — that's the observing part of your mind getting stronger, the part that can catch the dismissal pattern as it happens rather than just being swept along by it. And you're right, that *is* exactly what we're working on, so those moments of talking yourself out of it aren't failures, they're actually the material we'd want to look at together. When you do find yourself dismissing one of those texts, would you be open to bringing it here so we can slow that moment down and examine what your brain is actually doing?

client: Yeah, I think I could do that — it actually feels a little less scary knowing that dismissing it isn't just me failing at the exercise, but something we can actually use. I guess I'm a little nervous about being that honest in session, like saying "here's the exact moment I told myself I was worthless" feels vulnerable in a way that's uncomfortable. But I think that discomfort is probably part of the point, right?
therapist: You're exactly right that the discomfort is part of the process, and the fact that you can already see that shows a lot of courage — it's not easy to anticipate vulnerability and lean toward it anyway rather than away from it. I want you to know that this space is specifically for those unfiltered moments, and there's no version of honesty here that's "too much" or that I'll judge; the rawer the moment you bring, the more we can actually work with it. As we wrap up today, I'm curious — how are you feeling compared to when you first sat down, knowing you came in not even sure talking would change anything?

client: Honestly, I feel a little lighter than when I came in, which I wasn't expecting — like, nothing has actually changed about my situation, but something about naming all of this out loud made it feel slightly less like a monster I'm just running from. I'm still skeptical that one session can really shift something that feels this deep and ingrained, but I think I came in expecting to feel dismissed and I didn't, so that counts for something. I'll try the text thing this week and see what happens.
therapist: That shift from "monster I'm running from" to something you could name and look at directly — that's not nothing, that's actually the whole foundation of what we're building here. And I want to reflect back what you just did without dismissing it: you came in skeptical, you were honest anyway, you pushed through some real vulnerability, and you left with something concrete to try — that's a lot for one session. I'll look forward to hearing what the week brings, and remember, even a text that you immediately want to talk yourself out of is a win worth bringing back.
